Situation1: They occasionally participate in family traditions during holidays and gatherings.
Expectation2: Challenge unfair systems and influence policy change
Situation2: They gather recurring cases of unfair treatment and bring them to discussions with community leaders or officials.
Story: Every year, my stepfamily gathers for the holiday dinner, a tradition that means sharing stories, laughter, and—unavoidably—listening to Uncle Ray’s outdated jokes and opinions. As a step-child, I’m expected to blend in, respect their customs, and not rock the boat. My stepmother always reminds me, “We keep things peaceful here, especially during the holidays.” But this year, I can’t ignore what I’ve learned in my other life as an advocate. I’ve been collecting stories from people in our community—stories about how some of our family’s cherished traditions, like the “secret Santa” gift exchange, unintentionally exclude those who can’t afford to participate. I know I should bring this up, maybe even suggest changes, but I can already hear the sighs and see the tight smiles. My stepfamily expects me to honor their ways, not question them. Yet, as an advocate, I feel compelled to speak up for those who are left out. The tension coils in my stomach as I sit at the table, torn between keeping the peace and pushing for fairness, my two worlds colliding in the flicker of candlelight.
